title: Friday afternoon
hook: shopping, cooking and cleaning done early, so Shabbat can arrive calmly
tomorrow: Abraham left God mid-conversation to run to strangers. rude, or right?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two words in one breath: remember and observe, something done and something set down. Choose your Shabbat. Today, the hours just before it arrives.

Meal-prep videos make Sunday look serene: containers lined up, everything labeled, the week handled before it starts. The Talmud has its own version, for Fridays, and it's surprisingly hands-on. It names sages who had students and helpers, and still did the Shabbat preparations themselves. Rav Safra singed the head of the animal for the meal. Rava salted the fish. So why would a respected teacher do the kitchen work himself?
screen: `SUNDAY MEAL PREP, BUT FRIDAY.` → `RAV SAFRA SINGES. RAVA SALTS.` → `WHY DO IT YOURSELF?`

segments.voice: The Talmud's answer is a principle: a mitzvah you do yourself is greater than one done through someone else. And it gives these very sages as the example. Getting ready for Shabbat is part of honoring it, so they wanted their own hands in it. A second teaching makes it practical: whoever toils on the eve of Shabbat eats on Shabbat. In traditional practice nothing is cooked once the day begins, so tomorrow's rest is built today, hour by hour. That eve has its own name: erev Shabbat. Then a third sage shows what all the work is for. As the sun went down, Rabbi Hanina would wrap himself in his cloak and say: come, let's go out to greet the Shabbat queen. You can't go out to greet a queen while you're still scrubbing a pot by the door. That's ready before sunset. Not perfection; a calm arrival. The shopping, the cooking and the cleaning get pulled earlier, to Thursday if possible, so that when sunset comes there's nothing left to do but walk out to meet it. Something to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, a sage salted the Shabbat fish himself, on purpose.
screen: `A MITZVAH DONE YOURSELF.` · `TOIL ON THE EVE, EAT ON SHABBAT.` · `GO OUT TO GREET THE QUEEN.` · `PULL THE WORK EARLIER.` · then, large: `READY BEFORE SUNSET.`

segments.voice: Name one Friday task you could move earlier: the shopping, one dish, setting the table. Choose the exact moment you'll do it, Wednesday after work or Thursday before bed, and say the plan to yourself in one sentence. Then let yourself see Friday at sunset with that one thing already done.
screen: `ONE FRIDAY TASK.` · `MOVE IT EARLIER.` · `SEE SUNSET WITH IT DONE.`

segments.voice: Friday afternoon: erev Shabbat, the hours of getting ready, done early and with your own hands, so Shabbat can arrive calmly.
The line for this week: ready before sunset. Done early, so you can go out and greet it.

howItsDone: In observant homes Friday is erev Shabbat: food is cooked, the house cleaned, the table set and showers taken before sunset, and some families do much of the cooking on Thursday. Candle-lighting times are published for each town, a short while before sunset.

notes: Shabbat 119a / Kiddushin 41a: Rav Safra singed a head; Rava salted a fish (shibbuta). Confirm attributions and that Kiddushin 41a cites them for 'mitzvah bo yoter mi-shlucho'.
Rabbi Hanina's greeting ('come, let us go out to greet the Shabbat queen'), Shabbat 119a; paraphrased. Some texts attribute a parallel to Rabbi Yannai ('come, O bride'). Confirm.
'In traditional practice nothing is cooked once the day begins': general halakhic description; confirm phrasing.
